feedback: If the method omits what was kept constant, prompt: 'Could another person set up exactly the same test from this alone? What have you not told them to hold the same?'

If a results value appears without a unit or with inconsistent significant figures, flag it: 'A bare number isn't a measurement — add the SI unit and record values to the resolution of your instrument, keeping the precision consistent.'
If the conclusion only restates the hypothesis, prompt: 'Quote an actual value or trend from your data here — what in the evidence makes you say this?'
If the evaluation is a single line, prompt: 'Name one anomaly and classify one error as systematic or random, then give one concrete improvement.'
activities.intendedInsight: A scientific report is not a diary of what happened; each section has a distinct job, and together they present evidence and reasoning precisely enough for others to scrutinise.
learnerActions: Write a complete report with the conventional sections — aim, testable hypothesis, method, results, conclusion, evaluation — for an investigation you have actually run or been given full data for.
Draft the method as a numbered, unambiguous procedure that states what was kept constant (controlled variables), not as a past-tense story of what you did.
Build results tables and graphs with headed columns, SI units and correct significant figures throughout.
Write a conclusion that quotes specific values, a gradient, or a trend from your own data and states whether it supports the hypothesis — do not merely restate the hypothesis.
Write an evaluation that genuinely analyses reliability: identify anomalies, distinguish systematic from random error, and propose specific improvements.
Before finalising, check each section against stated success criteria for that section.
activities.title: Report studio: compose the six sections with built-in checks

feedback: If a learner only flags presentation (spelling, layout), redirect: 'Those are surface fixes — does the evidence actually support the conclusion? Is the method repeatable?'
If an overreaching conclusion is missed, prompt: 'Does the data cover the claim being made, or has the author gone beyond what was measured?'
activities.intendedInsight: Peer review chiefly scrutinises method, evidence, and reasoning — whether the conclusions are actually justified — rather than spelling or formatting. Learning to spot overreach and vagueness in others' work sharpens it in your own.
learnerActions: Read a sample report containing deliberate flaws (a vague method, an overreaching conclusion, an unsupported claim, a missing control, missing units).
Mark each weakness and explain against explicit criteria why it fails — e.g. 'this conclusion claims more than the data shows', 'this method cannot be reproduced because…'.
Compare a gold-standard report and a flawed one section by section, articulating what makes each section strong or weak.
Suggest the specific revision each flaw requires.
activities.title: Review desk: critique a flawed report against criteria

feedback: If a learner locates trust in the scientist's care, honesty, or fame, respond: 'Even careful, honest scientists make errors or hit flukes. Independent checking is precisely what catches what they cannot see themselves.'

If a learner dismisses replication as pointless repetition or treats published work as final proof, respond: 'Scientific knowledge is provisional. Replication is what upgrades a claim from tentative to trusted — and it can also overturn one.'

If a learner reduces peer review to checking spelling or formatting, respond: 'Peer review mainly scrutinises the method, evidence, and reasoning — whether the conclusions are justified — not just the presentation.'
Reinforce a full answer: 'You located reliability in independent reproducibility rather than authority, and you recognised that a result no one can reproduce should be doubted.'
activities.intendedInsight: Reliability comes from independent scrutiny and reproduction by OTHER labs — not from the authority, fame, or honesty of the scientist. A result earns trust only when others independently obtain it; failure to replicate is grounds to doubt the claim. All scientific knowledge stays provisional: independent confirmation makes us more confident in a claim, but later evidence can still revise or overturn it.
learnerActions: Respond to the prompt: 'A scientist publishes a surprising result. Before other scientists accept it, the work goes through peer review, and other labs try to replicate it. Why aren't the scientist's own careful report and honest word enough — what do peer review and independent replication add? And what would it mean if no one else could reproduce the result?'

In a role-play, defend your own report to a reviewer/editor who probes: 'Is your method reproducible? Does your conclusion overreach the data? What would a replication need?' Then swap seats and review the character's flawed manuscript.

Argue through the discriminating cases: What does a reviewer check that the original scientist might have missed? If three other labs get a different result, what should happen to the claim? Does a scientist being famous and careful make replication unnecessary? Why is a result only one lab can ever produce treated with suspicion?
activities.title: Why peer review and replication make knowledge reliable

feedback: For a mis-ordered structure, prompt: 'What must be stated before results can be interpreted?'
For a 'peer review = proofreading' choice, respond: 'Reviewers judge whether the science and reasoning hold up, not the spelling.'
For a spot-the-weakness item, confirm the specific flaw: 'Correct — this conclusion asserts a result without quoting any value from the data.'
activities.intendedInsight: The conventions of report structure and the facts about peer review and replication can be checked quickly, but they are prerequisites for — not a substitute for — actually composing and defending a report.
learnerActions: Match each piece of content to the report section it belongs in (e.g. 'what was kept constant' → method; 'the gradient of the weight–mass graph was 9.8 N/kg' → results/conclusion).
Put the sections of a report into the correct order.
Identify the purpose of peer review and of replication from short options, distinguishing scrutiny of reasoning from proofreading.
Spot the weakness in a short sample method or conclusion snippet (e.g. a conclusion that cites no data).
activities.title: Check component knowledge of conventions and nature of science
